items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: You are paralysed multiple times every night
items.claim: During REM sleep, when most dreams occur, motor neurons to your skeletal muscles are actively inhibited. You cannot move. This is REM atonia — and when it fails, people act out their dreams.
items.prompt: Why does the brain paralyse you while dreaming?

options.text: To prevent acting out dream content — the same brain regions that command movement are active in REM as in waking, but spinal motor neurons are blocked from receiving the signals
To stop heart rate from rising

items.reveal_title: REM behavior disorder and Schenck's discovery
items.reveal:
The brainstem (specifically the pons and medulla) sends inhibitory signals to spinal motor neurons during REM. The motor cortex fires in patterns resembling waking; the descending commands reach the spinal cord but cannot trigger muscle contraction.

In REM Behavior Disorder (Schenck 1986), this paralysis fails. Patients punch, kick, vocalise and act out vivid dreams. RBD is strongly associated with later Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia — the brainstem regions controlling REM atonia degrade early in these conditions.

Narcolepsy with cataplexy is the opposite failure: REM-style atonia intrudes into waking life, triggered by emotion. Modafinil and other treatments stabilise the boundary between sleep states.
items.why: Sleep is imagined as 'off'. REM sleep is intensely active — and the body needs active suppression to prevent the brain's instructions reaching the muscles.

items.title: Enzymes don't 'fit' substrates — they fit transition states
items.claim: The textbook 'lock and key' model says enzymes have an active site that matches the substrate. Real enzymes are much more interesting: they bind the TRANSITION STATE of the reaction more tightly than the substrate or product.
items.prompt: Why does binding the transition state make a better catalyst?

options.text: It doesn't matter what the enzyme binds tightly
Stabilising the highest-energy point in the reaction lowers the activation energy; an enzyme that binds the transition state by 1000-fold relative to substrate accelerates the reaction by 1000-fold
Binding the substrate tightly always speeds up reactions
The substrate spontaneously becomes the transition state

items.reveal_title: Linus Pauling's prediction and modern enzyme design
items.reveal:
Pauling proposed in 1948 that enzymes catalyse reactions by binding most strongly to the transition state, lowering the activation energy.

Direct evidence: 'transition state analogues' — stable molecules that mimic the transition state's geometry — bind enzymes 10 to 10,000 times more tightly than the substrates themselves. Many drugs are designed this way (statins like atorvastatin mimic the transition state of HMG-CoA reductase).

Catalytic antibodies, raised against transition state analogues, can catalyse reactions for which no natural enzyme exists (Schultz, Lerner, 1986). De novo enzyme design (Baker lab, 2008 onward) explicitly engineers active sites to fit predicted transition states.

The induced-fit model (Koshland 1958) and the transition-state model are both refinements of the original lock-and-key.
items.why: Lock-and-key implies stable binding of stable molecules. Enzymes catalyse by binding unstable, fleeting transition states — a much subtler picture.
